A steel rod and an aluminium rod of identical length and cross-section are joined end to end, with insulated sides and ideal contact. The steel end is at 100°C and the aluminium end at 20°C. Conductivities are 80 and 220 W/(m·K). Find the steady junction temperature.
Express the answer in this unit: °C

Before the final answer line, give a concise worked solution with the governing equation, substitution with units, and the calculation.

The joint stores no energy in steady state, so the two rods transmit the same heat rate. With common A/L, Fourier's law reduces to 80(100−T) = 220(T−20). The result is 41.3°C. A check is the larger temperature drop on the steel side: for equal geometry, the lower conductivity requires a steeper gradient.
FINAL = 41.3

title: Calculating Temperature: Calorimetry with an Ideal Gas
question: In an insulated rigid vessel 12.0 mol of diatomic ideal gas at 95°C contacts 300 g of gallium at its melting point of 30°C. At equilibrium, 202 g have melted. Find the gallium heat of fusion using C_V = 5R/2 and R = 8.31 J/(mol·K).
worked_solution: Since some solid gallium remains, solid and liquid coexist and the final temperature is 30°C. The gas does no expansion work at fixed volume. Its energy loss is nC_V(95−30) ≈ 16.2 kJ. The metal was already at the melting point, so this energy melts only the 0.202 kg that changed phase. Dividing by that mass gives 80.2 kJ/kg.

title: Polishing a Fitting
question: A 0.50 kg copper part is polished against 20 N of friction at 1.0 m/s for 120 s. Estimate the temperature rise if the copper retains all frictional work, using c = 390 J/(kg·K). Give the nearest kelvin.
worked_solution: The surfaces slide 120 m, so the dissipated mechanical energy is 20×120 = 2400 J. Set this equal to the part's sensible heat gain, mcΔT. Its heat capacity is 195 J/K, giving a rise of 12 K to the nearest kelvin. Heat sharing with the tool would reduce the rise.

title: Vaporizing Water
question: One gram of boiling water absorbs 2260 J while turning into vapour against 1.01e5 Pa, increasing volume by 1.67e−3 m³. Find the internal energy increase using the closed-system first law.
worked_solution: Separate the heat absorbed from the work done by the expanding sample. The boundary work is pΔV = 1.01e5×1.67e−3 ≈ 169 J since Pa·m³ is a joule. The internal energy change is Q−W ≈ 2260−169 = 2.09e3 J, positive but smaller than the heat input.

title: Calculating the Thickness of a Nonreflective Lens Coating
question: Light of vacuum wavelength 500 nm strikes a MgF₂ coating (n = 1.38) on glass (n = 1.52) from air at normal incidence. What is the least positive coating thickness that minimizes the reflected light?
worked_solution: Reflection from the air-to-coating and coating-to-glass interfaces produces the same π phase reversal at each. Their reflection phase shifts therefore cancel in the relative phase. Destructive interference needs the round-trip optical distance 2nt to equal half a wavelength at lowest order. Thus t = 500/(4×1.38) = 90.6 nm. This condition sets the minimum even if the amplitudes are unequal.

title: Soap Bubbles
question: A free soap film of index 1.333 has air on both sides. At normal incidence, find the second smallest positive thickness giving bright reflected light at a vacuum wavelength of 650 nm.
worked_solution: Only the first reflection, from air to the denser film, adds a π phase shift. Bright reflection therefore requires an odd half-wavelength of round-trip optical path. The thicknesses start at λ/(4n), then 3λ/(4n). Select the second member: 3×650/(4×1.333) ≈ 366 nm.

title: Precise Distance Measurements by Michelson Interferometer
question: A Michelson interferometer uses 630 nm light in air. Moving one mirror changes the count at a fixed viewing point by one whole fringe. Find the magnitude of mirror displacement.
worked_solution: Light travels to the moving mirror and back, so displacement x changes the path difference by 2x. One complete fringe corresponds to one wavelength of path change. Solving 2x = 630 nm gives x = 315 nm.

title: Measuring the Refractive Index of a Gas
question: A Michelson interferometer arm contains an initially evacuated 2.0 cm cell. Filling it with a gas shifts 122 fringes at vacuum wavelength 632.8 nm. Calculate the refractive index of the filled cell gas.
worked_solution: The window and reference-arm optical paths are unchanged between readings. The beam makes two passes through the gas, so the added optical path is 2L(n−1). Set this to 122λ, giving n = 1 + 122×632.8e−9/(2×0.020) = 1.0019. The measured small quantity is the excess over unity.

title: Speed of Light in Jewelry
question: For light of the wavelength at which zircon has refractive index 1.923, find its phase speed. Take vacuum light speed as 3.00e8 m/s.
worked_solution: The phase refractive index is the ratio of vacuum speed to the phase speed in the crystal. Thus v = c/n = 3.00e8/1.923 = 1.56e8 m/s. The units remain those of speed and n above unity makes v less than c.

title: Determining the Index of Refraction
question: A ray goes from air into an unknown medium. Incidence and refraction angles measured from the normal are 30.0° and 22.0°, respectively. Estimate the medium's index assuming n_air = 1.00.
worked_solution: Snell's law equates n₁ sin θ₁ and n₂ sin θ₂. Isolate the unknown index and take the ratio sin 30°/sin 22°, about 1.33. Bending toward the normal is consistent with entry into the higher-index medium.

title: Determining a Critical Angle
question: A ray travels inside a transparent polymer of index 1.49 toward air (index 1.00). At what incidence angle from the normal does the transmitted ray first become grazing?

question: White light enters crown glass from air at 43.2° to the normal. The glass indices are 1.512 for red and 1.530 for violet. Find the separation of the refracted rays to the nearest tenth of a degree.

title: Photoelectric Effect for Silver
question: Silver has a work function of 4.73 eV. Find the longest vacuum wavelength capable of single-photon photoemission, using hc = 1240 eV·nm.
worked_solution: At threshold the fastest emitted electron has zero excess kinetic energy, so the photon energy equals the work function. Rearranging hc/λ = 4.73 eV gives λ = 1240/4.73 ≈ 262 nm. Longer wavelengths would supply less energy.

title: Work Function and Cut-Off Frequency
question: Illumination at 180 nm produces photoelectrons from an unknown metal; a retarding potential of magnitude 0.80 V stops the most energetic electrons. Determine the threshold frequency. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm and h = 4.136e−15 eV·s.
worked_solution: The stopping measurement supplies K_max = 0.80 eV. The incoming photons carry 1240/180 ≈ 6.89 eV; the work function takes the remainder, 6.09 eV. At threshold the electron just escapes, so hν₀ = φ. Dividing 6.09 eV by h gives 1.47e15 Hz.

title: Niobium Wire
question: A long cylindrical niobium wire of radius 0.25 mm carries 300 A. What magnetic flux density does its own current produce immediately outside its surface? Use μ₀ = 4πe−7 T·m/A and neglect end effects.
worked_solution: An Amperian circle just outside the wire encloses its full current, irrespective of its radial current distribution. Cylindrical symmetry makes B constant on this path, so B(2πr) = μ₀I. Substitution of r = 0.25e−3 m and I = 300 A gives 0.24 T.

title: X-Ray Diffraction with Salt Crystals
question: Planes of spacing 0.252 nm in salt produce a first-order Bragg maximum at a glancing angle of 18.1°. Determine the incident wavelength.
worked_solution: For waves scattered from adjacent planes the path difference is 2d sin θ, where θ is measured from the planes. At the first maximum this equals one wavelength. Thus λ = 2×0.252×sin(18.1°) nm ≈ 0.157 nm.

title: Heat Transfer between Substances at Different Temperatures
question: A 360.0 g steel bar is quenched in 425 g of water initially at 24.0°C. The measured common temperature is 42.7°C. Treat the bar and water as isolated, with specific heats 0.449 and 4.184 J/(g·K). Find the bar's initial temperature to the nearest degree.
worked_solution: The water gains 425×4.184×18.7 ≈ 33,250 J. The bar loses the same heat; its heat capacity is 360.0×0.449 ≈ 161.6 J/K. It must have cooled by about 206 K before reaching 42.7°C. Add the drop to the final temperature to obtain 248°C.

title: Identifying a Metal by Measuring Specific Heat
question: A 59.7 g metal specimen at 100.0°C is immersed in 60.0 g of water at 22.0°C. The final mixture is at 28.5°C. Neglect container heat capacity and losses, and take c_water = 4.184 J/(g·K). Estimate the metal's specific heat.
worked_solution: Use the water as the calibrated heat receiver. Its gain is 60.0×4.184×6.5 J. The metal mass cools through 71.5 K, so 59.7×71.5×c_m equals that gain. Rearranging gives about 0.38 J/(g·K), positive because both the heat lost and the metal temperature drop were used as magnitudes.

title: Heat Produced by an Exothermic Reaction
question: In a constant-pressure calorimeter 50.0 mL each of 1 M acid and 1 M base are mixed at 22.0°C and the mixture reaches 28.9°C. Treat the total volume as additive, density as 1.00 g/mL, and c as 4.184 J/(g·K). Find the signed reaction heat in kJ. Ignore other heat exchanges.
worked_solution: The solution has mass 100 g. Its temperature rises 6.9 K and it therefore absorbs 100×4.184×6.9 ≈ 2.9 kJ. In the calorimeter energy balance the reaction is the donor, so q_reaction = −q_solution = −2.9 kJ for the whole sample.

title: Heat Flow in an Instant Ice Pack
question: Dissolving 3.21 g of salt in 50.0 g of water changes the temperature from 24.9°C to 20.3°C. The entire resulting solution has specific heat 4.184 J/(g·K). Neglect the vessel and environment. Find the signed heat absorbed by dissolution, in kJ to two significant digits.
worked_solution: The measured cooling refers to the final solution, so use its full 53.21 g mass. Its sensible heat change is 53.21×4.184×(20.3−24.9) ≈ −1024 J. Conservation makes the dissolution heat equal and opposite. The endothermic process absorbs approximately +1.0 kJ.

title: Using Enthalpy of Combustion
question: Approximate a 1.00 L liquid fuel sample as isooctane, with density 0.692 g/mL, molar mass 114 g/mol and combustion enthalpy −5460 kJ/mol. What is the magnitude of heat released in complete combustion?
worked_solution: The heat is specified per mole, so first convert the volume to 692 g, then divide by 114 g/mol to obtain 6.07 mol. Multiply by 5460 kJ/mol to obtain 3.31e4 kJ released. The signed enthalpy change of the fuel reaction is negative while the requested magnitude is positive.

title: Stepwise Calculation of Δ H f ° Using Hess’s Law
question: Forming one mole of FeCl₂(s) from Fe(s) and Cl₂(g) has ΔH° = −341.8 kJ. Adding half a mole of Cl₂ to this FeCl₂ gives one mole of FeCl₃(s) with ΔH° = −57.7 kJ. Find the standard molar formation enthalpy of FeCl₃(s).
worked_solution: Seek a formation reaction with one mole of FeCl3 as product. Adding Fe + Cl2 -> FeCl2 to FeCl2 + 0.5 Cl2 -> FeCl3 cancels FeCl2 without reversing either equation. The net reactants are Fe and 1.5 Cl2 in their standard states. Each step is used once, so add its signed enthalpy once: -341.8 + (-57.7) = -399.5 kJ per mole of FeCl3. The net reaction uses three chlorine atoms per formula unit, which checks the summed stoichiometry.

title: Estimating Enthalpy of Vaporization
question:
The saturation pressure of isooctane is measured at two temperatures.

| T (K) | Pressure (kPa) |
| --- | --- |
| 307.2 | 10.0 |
| 372.0 | 100.0 |

Assume ideal vapour, negligible liquid molar volume and constant enthalpy of vaporization. Estimate the molar vaporization enthalpy using R = 8.3145 J/(mol·K).
worked_solution: For coexistence of liquid and vapour, integrate the Clausius–Clapeyron relation between the two measurements. The denominator is 1/307.2−1/372.0 K⁻¹ and the numerator is R ln(100/10). Their ratio is about 33,800 J/mol, or 33.8 kJ/mol. Pressure units cancel and the positive sign agrees with endothermic vaporization.

title: Estimating Temperature (or Vapor Pressure)
question: Benzene boils at 353.3 K under 101.3 kPa. Estimate the boiling temperature at 83.4 kPa if ΔH_vap = 30.8 kJ/mol remains constant. Take R = 8.3145 J/(mol·K) and ideal vapour behaviour.
worked_solution: At boiling the vapour pressure equals the external pressure. The integrated vapour-pressure relation gives 1/T₂ = 1/353.3 − (8.3145/30,800)ln(83.4/101.3). Invert after performing the subtraction to obtain about 346.9 K. The lower pressure lets boiling occur at a lower temperature.

title: Total Heat Needed to Change Temperature and Phase for a Substance
question: At 1 atm convert 135 g of ice at −15°C into steam at 120°C. The specific heats of ice, water and steam are 2.09, 4.18 and 1.86 J/(g·K); fusion and vaporization enthalpies are 6.01 and 40.67 kJ/mol. Use M = 18.02 g/mol. Find the total heat. Report two significant figures.
worked_solution: Follow the material through five stages. Warm the ice to 0°C (4.23 kJ), melt 135/18.02 mol (45.0 kJ), then warm liquid water to 100°C (56.4 kJ). The same number of moles must vaporize, requiring about 304.7 kJ. Finally superheat the steam by 20 K (5.02 kJ). Adding the unrounded terms gives 415.4 kJ, or 4.2e2 kJ to two significant figures. Latent heat contributes even while the temperature is stationary.

title: Calculation of Atomic Radius and Density for Metals, Part 1
question: Alpha polonium forms a simple cubic lattice with edge length 336 pm. In the touching-sphere model, what is its atomic radius?
worked_solution: In simple cubic packing the nearest neighbours lie along each cell edge. One edge joins the centres of two touching atoms, so it spans two radii. Thus r = a/2 = 336/2 = 168 pm.

question: Calcium forms an FCC unit cell of side 558.8 pm. Use 40.078 g/mol and 6.022e23 atoms/mol to calculate its crystal density in g/cm³.

title: Calculation of Ionic Radii
question: LiCl has the rock-salt structure with unit-cell edge 0.514 nm. Assume the chloride anions touch each other in their FCC sublattice. What chloride radius follows?
worked_solution: Consider one cube face. Corner and face-centred chloride ions align along its diagonal, spanning four radii across a distance √2 a. The model therefore gives r_Cl = 0.514√2/4 = 0.182 nm. Contact along the cube edge would involve unlike ions and would require the cation radius.

LiCl has the rock-salt structure with unit-cell edge 0.514 nm. Assume the chloride anions touch each other in their FCC sublattice. What chloride radius follows?
Express the answer in this unit: nm

Before the final answer line, give a concise worked solution with the governing equation, substitution with units, and the calculation.

Consider one cube face. Corner and face-centred chloride ions align along its diagonal, spanning four radii across a distance √2 a. The model therefore gives r_Cl = 0.514√2/4 = 0.182 nm. Contact along the cube edge would involve unlike ions and would require the cation radius.

title: Using the Bragg Equation
question: Copper gives a first-order X-ray peak at the Bragg angle θ = 25.25° with incident wavelength 0.1315 nm. What spacing does this determine for the reflecting planes?
worked_solution: Constructive scattering requires adjacent planes to add one wavelength of extra path at first order. Hence d = λ/(2 sin θ). The stated angle is already the Bragg angle, so use 25.25° directly. The resulting spacing is 0.154 nm.

title: Application of Henry’s Law
question: Water at 20°C dissolves 1.38e−3 mol/L oxygen when the oxygen partial pressure is 101.3 kPa. At the same temperature what concentration equilibrates with 20.7 kPa oxygen in the dilute Henry-law regime?
worked_solution: The Henry coefficient at this fixed temperature cancels from C₂/C₁ = p₂/p₁. Use the oxygen partial pressures in both states, obtaining 1.38e−3×20.7/101.3 = 2.82e−4 mol/L. The concentration is about one fifth of the original, as expected from the pressure ratio.

title: Calculating Mole Fraction and Molality
question: A coolant contains 2220 g ethylene glycol (62.07 g/mol) and 2000 g water. Determine the molality of the glycol expressed per kg of water.
worked_solution: Molality uses moles of solute per mass of solvent. The mixture has 2220/62.07 ≈ 35.77 mol glycol and 2.000 kg of water. Their ratio is 17.9 mol/kg. Using the combined mass of the liquid would describe a different concentration.

title: Molality and Molarity Conversions
question: A solution contains 0.556 mol/L of a nonvolatile solute of molar mass 180.2 g/mol. The solution density is 1.04 kg/L and the balance is water. What is its solute molality to two decimal places?
worked_solution: Choose one litre of solution. It contains 0.556 mol solute in 1.04 kg total. The solute accounts for 0.556×0.1802 ≈ 0.1002 kg, leaving 0.9398 kg solvent. The molality is 0.556/0.9398 ≈ 0.59 mol/kg.

title: Calculation of a Vapor Pressure
question: At 40°C, 184.4 g ethanol and 92.1 g effectively nonvolatile glycerin form an ideal solution. Their molar masses are 46.069 and 92.094 g/mol and pure ethanol has vapour pressure 0.178 atm. What is the total vapour pressure?
worked_solution: Only ethanol has appreciable vapour pressure. Raoult's law multiplies its pure-component pressure by its liquid mole fraction. There are about 4.00 mol ethanol and 1.00 mol glycerin, so x_ethanol ≈ 0.800. The pressure is 0.800×0.178 ≈ 0.142 atm, below the pure-solvent value.

title: The Integrated Rate Law for a Second-Order Reaction
question: A dimerizing monomer starts at 0.200 mol/L and follows −d[A]/dt = k[A]² with k = 0.0576 L/(mol·min). What concentration remains after 10.0 min?

Inverting 5.576 gives 0.179 mol/L. The definition of k in the question already refers to monomer disappearance.

title: Converting Current to Moles of Electrons
question: A current of 10.23 A flows for exactly one hour through a cell depositing silver from Ag⁺. With full current efficiency, F = 96,485 C/mol and M_Ag = 107.9 g/mol, how much silver is plated?
worked_solution: Integrate the steady current over 3600 s to obtain 36,828 C. Division by F gives about 0.3817 mol electrons. The cathode reaction consumes one electron per silver atom, so the same molar amount deposits. Multiplying by 107.9 g/mol yields 41.19 g to the given precision.

title: Time Required for Deposition
question: A uniform 0.010 mm chromium coating is required on 3.3 m². Plate from Cr³⁺ at 33.46 A with full current efficiency. Use ρ = 7.19 g/cm³, molar mass 52.00 g/mol and F = 96,485 C/mol. Find deposition time in hours.
worked_solution: Start with geometry: area is 33,000 cm² and thickness is 0.0010 cm, so the deposit occupies 33 cm³. Density converts this to about 237 g or 4.56 mol Cr. Each mole deposited from Cr³⁺ needs three moles of electrons, giving roughly 1.32e6 C. Divide by the current to obtain seconds and then by 3600 for hours, about 11.0 h. The charge factor comes from ionic valence, independently of film geometry.

title: Equilibrium Constants, Standard Cell Potentials, and Standard Free Energy Changes
question: For 2Ag⁺ + Fe → 2Ag + Fe²⁺, the standard reduction potentials are +0.7996 V for silver and −0.447 V for iron. Find the standard cell voltage.
worked_solution: Silver ions gain electrons at the cathode and iron supplies electrons at the anode. Both tabulated numbers are reduction potentials, so subtract the iron value from the silver value. Voltages are intensive and are not multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients. The result is 0.7996−(−0.447) = 1.247 V to three decimals.

title: Concentration Cells
question: Two zinc electrodes contact ideal Zn²⁺ solutions of 0.10 M and 0.50 M at 25°C. For the spontaneous orientation of this concentration cell, find the voltage using the base-10 Nernst coefficient 0.0592 V.
worked_solution: The standard electrode potentials cancel because both half-cells use the same metal. Reduction favours the higher zinc-ion concentration and oxidation raises the lower concentration. With two electrons transferred, E = (0.0592/2)log₁₀(0.50/0.10), which gives a positive 0.021 V.

title: Calculation of a First-order Rate Constant using Half-Life
question: At 40°C a species undergoing first-order decomposition reaches half its initial concentration after 2.16e4 s. Find its rate constant.
worked_solution: For first-order decay the surviving fraction is exp(−kt). At the measured half-life this is 1/2. Taking logarithms gives k = ln 2/(2.16e4 s) = 3.21e−5 s⁻¹. The initial concentration cancels.

title: Occupancy of Tetrahedral Holes
question: Sulfide ions form a close-packed sublattice with two tetrahedral holes per sulfide ion. Zinc ions occupy one half of those holes. What number of zinc ions occurs per sulfide ion?
worked_solution: Count on a basis of N sulfide ions. They provide 2N tetrahedral sites, of which half are occupied, giving N zinc ions. The number ratio Zn:S is therefore N/N = 1, consistent with ZnS stoichiometry.

title: Calculation of Osmotic Pressure
question: An ideal dilute aqueous solution of a nondissociating solute has concentration 0.30 mol/L at 310 K. Find the osmotic pressure in atm with R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K).
worked_solution: Osmotic pressure counts independently dissolved particles. With no dissociation the particle concentration is 0.30 mol/L. Compute Π = cRT = 0.30×0.08206×310 atm, or 7.6 atm. The gas constant and molarity already share litre and mole units.

title: Using Enthalpy of Vaporization
question: Liquid water at 37°C evaporates isothermally. For a sample of 1.5 kg use molar mass 18 g/mol and enthalpy of vaporization 43.46 kJ/mol at this temperature. What heat does the water absorb?
worked_solution: An isothermal phase change requires latent heat. Convert 1.5 kg to 1500 g and divide by 18 g/mol to get about 83 mol. At 43.46 kJ per mole the heat is about 3.6e3 kJ. No sensible-heat term is required because the temperature is fixed.

question: At 400 and 500 K the standard formation reaction of crystalline Vanadium Oxide (O5V2) has log₁₀ Kf values 179.52 and 139.096. Assuming nearly constant reaction enthalpy and the same standard phases across this interval, estimate ΔfH°. Use R=8.31446 J/(mol K).
worked_solution:
The integrated van 't Hoff relation is ln(K₂/K₁)=−ΔH°(1/T₂−1/T₁)/R. Multiply the difference of decimal logarithms by ln 10. The slope versus inverse temperature gives the enthalpy with the minus sign. Numerically, -8.31446 * log(10) * (139.096 - 179.52) / (1 / 500 - 1 / 400) / 1000 ≈ -1547.8 kJ/mol.
Check the sign using the temperature dependence of K: an exothermic formation reaction has a smaller equilibrium constant at the higher temperature.

question: A tested steel has engineering yield strength 1136.8 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 1205.8 MPa, and elongation to fracture 22.5%. Design a round 8 mm diameter tie with safety factors of 1.5 against yielding and 2 against ultimate failure. What is the allowable axial load?
worked_solution: The tie must satisfy both strength criteria. The yield limit permits 1136.8/1.5=757.87 MPa; the ultimate limit permits 1205.8/2=602.90 MPa. The lower value is the ultimate-strength constraint. The original cross section is π(8 mm)²/4=50.265 mm². Since 1 MPa=1 N/mm², its allowable load is 602.90×50.265/1000=30.305 kN. At that load the safety factors against yield and ultimate strength are 1.886 and 2.000, respectively, meeting both requirements.

question: For a dense random polycrystal of K2O2, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 31.891 and 15.58 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. Two small-amplitude bulk waves propagate in the same medium. What is the ratio of the longitudinal speed to the transverse speed?
worked_solution:
The longitudinal wave modulus is K+4G/3 and the shear wave modulus is G. Both speeds involve the same density, which cancels in their ratio. Thus vL/vT=√[(31.891+4×15.58/3)/15.58]. Numerically, sqrt((31.891 + 4 * 15.58 / 3) / 15.58) ≈ 1.8385.
Both waves propagate in the same mass density. Longitudinal compression excites a bulk response in addition to shear, so it must be faster here.

question: For the following operating case, crude oil volume = 158.99 L; crude oil calorific value = 40000000 J/L; efficiency = 42 %; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg·℃); temperature rise of water = 20 ℃. Use constant specific heat and assume no phase change in the heated sample. Treat the given fuel as completely burned. Use the ratio of useful output to supplied input for the indicated conversion. Determine the mass of water.
worked_solution: Heat released by complete combustion of crude oil = crude oil volume × crude oil calorific value. Substitution gives (158.99 L) × (40000000 J / L), or 6.3596e+09 J. Heat absorbed by water = heat released by complete combustion of crude oil × efficiency. Substitution gives (6359600000 J) × (42 %), or 2.671032e+09 J. Mass of water = heat absorbed by water / (specific heat capacity of water × temperature rise of water). Substitution gives (2671032000 J) / ((4200 J / (kg·℃)) × (20 ℃)), or 31798 kg. The result is approximately 31798 kg.

question: For a dense random polycrystal of Hf2Pd, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 136.801694 and 55.1568909 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. A rod 75 mm long with section 20 mm² is loaded quasistatically from zero to 950 N in tension. Find the stored elastic energy.
worked_solution:
First convert the two aggregate moduli to Young's modulus: E=9KG/(3K+G)=145.867 GPa. The stiffness is EA/L in N/mm after converting GPa to MPa. Linear loading stores half the final load times extension, U=F²L/(2EA). One N mm is one mJ. Numerically, 950 ^ 2 * 75 / (2 * 20 * 1000 * (9 * 136.801694 * 55.1568909 / (3 * 136.801694 + 55.1568909))) ≈ 11.601 mJ.
For a straight-line load–extension curve its area is half the final load times the final extension. N·mm converts directly to mJ.

question: A DFPT stress-form piezoelectric tensor for KBF4 gives e33 = 0.13976 C/m² in Cartesian axes. At zero electric field impose a compressive normal strain of magnitude 0.10% along axis 3, with all other strain components held at zero. What signed polarization change along axis 3 is predicted in µC/m²?
worked_solution:
Use the direct effect at fixed electric field, ΔP_i=Σ e_ik ε_k. Here only ε_3=-0.001 contributes. The given coefficient already uses polarization per unit strain. Multiplying 0.13976 by -0.001 gives C/m²; convert by 10⁶. Numerically, 0.13976 * -0.001 * 1000000.0 ≈ -139.76 µC/m².
A tensile-to-compressive strain reversal reverses the sign of the polarization increment at fixed electric field. Percent strain must be divided by 100 before contracting the tensor.

question: A homogeneous Pb0.94Sr0.04TeNa0.02 leg operates near 700 K. Treat the reported coefficients as constant over a small temperature difference. Electrical conductivity is 471.0 S/cm. question: For crystalline Lithium Tetrahydroborate (H4BLi) at standard pressure, evaluated at 500 K, S°=122.48 J/(mol K) and H°(T)−H°(298.15 K)=18.349 kJ/mol. Calculate −[G°(T)−H°(298.15 K)]/T.

question: Use an effective, transparent, nonmagnetic optical medium for KZnF3, with trace-averaged electronic relative permittivity 2.35. In the dispersion-free approximation, what physical film thickness gives a quarter-wave optical thickness at a vacuum wavelength of 620 nm? Ignore absorption.
worked_solution:
Use the electronic response at optical frequencies. The effective index is n=√ε∞. The optical path nd must equal λ₀/4; use the vacuum wavelength once. Therefore d=620/(4n) nm. Numerically, 620 / (4 * sqrt(2.35)) ≈ 101.11 nm.
The wavelength inside the film is shorter than in vacuum by the index factor. The geometric thickness must be one quarter of that internal wavelength.

Use an effective, transparent, nonmagnetic optical medium for KZnF3, with trace-averaged electronic relative permittivity 2.35. In the dispersion-free approximation, what physical film thickness gives a quarter-wave optical thickness at a vacuum wavelength of 620 nm? Ignore absorption.
Express the answer in this unit: nm

Before the final answer line, give a concise worked solution with the governing equation, substitution with units, and the calculation.

Use the electronic response at optical frequencies. The effective index is n=√ε∞. The optical path nd must equal λ₀/4; use the vacuum wavelength once. Therefore d=620/(4n) nm. Numerically, 620 / (4 * sqrt(2.35)) ≈ 101.11 nm.
The wavelength inside the film is shorter than in vacuum by the index factor. The geometric thickness must be one quarter of that internal wavelength.
FINAL = 101.11

question: An open boiler contains 500 kg of water initially at 20 °C. It burns 21 kg of coke with a lower heating value of 30 MJ/kg; 20% reaches the water. At this pressure water boils at 100 °C. Use cp = 4.20 kJ/(kg K) and latent heat = 2.26 MJ/kg. Neglect vessel heat capacity and all further losses. Determine the final water temperature.
worked_solution: The useful energy is 21×30×0.20 = 126 MJ. Reaching saturation requires 500×4.20×(100−20) kJ = 168 MJ. The budget falls below that threshold. All useful energy heats liquid, so ΔT=126000/(500×4.20)=60 K and the final temperature is 80 °C, below boiling.

question: Apply the P critical flow relation with the following quantities. P = 1400000 Pa (Stagnation pressure of a fluid with Ma=1); k = 1.289 (dimensionless) (Isentropic exponent). In the units specified, use result = P * (2.0 / (k + 1.0)) ^ (k / (k - 1.0)). Determine the critical flow pressure at Ma=1 in Pa.
worked_solution:
The critical state is the sonic section of isentropic flow. Its static pressure is a fraction of the upstream stagnation pressure.
result = 1400000 * (2.0 / (1.289 + 1.0)) ^ (1.289 / (1.289 - 1.0)) = 766813 Pa.

question: A single phase of crystalline Beryllium Sulfate, Alpha (BeO4S) at constant pressure has endpoint molar heat capacities 126.817 and 137.988 J/(mol K) at 600 and 700 K. Estimate the molar heat input over this interval assuming linear variation of Cp and no phase change.
worked_solution:
At constant pressure q_p=ΔH. Integrate Cp(T), approximating it with a straight line. The mean is (126.817+137.988)/2 J/(mol K). Multiply by 100 K and convert from J to kJ. Numerically, (126.817 + 137.988) * 0.05 ≈ 13.24 kJ/mol.
For linear Cp the heat is the area of a trapezoid. It lies between the two endpoint heat capacities multiplied by the temperature rise.

question: The calculated elastic data for V5Sb4 give normal compliance trace 0.0342001574, sum S12+S13+S23 = -0.0114838709, and engineering shear compliance trace 0.0417477982, in GPa⁻¹. Determine the bulk modulus of the uniform-stress aggregate.
worked_solution:
Hydrostatic loading gives a volume compliance S11+S22+S33+2(S12+S13+S23). Its inverse is K_R. Numerically K_R = 1/[0.0342001574+2(-0.0114838709)] GPa. Numerically, 1 / (0.0342001574 + 2 * -0.0114838709) ≈ 89.028 GPa.
Hydrostatic loading applies equal normal stresses and no shear stresses. This is the uniform-stress estimate; a uniform-strain stiffness average describes another bound.

question: Use an effective, transparent, nonmagnetic optical medium for Si3N4, with trace-averaged electronic relative permittivity 4.26. At vacuum wavelength 1.55 µm, find the additional single-pass phase in radians through a 2.0 µm slab relative to the same distance in vacuum. Report the unwrapped phase.
worked_solution:
Use the electronic response at optical frequencies. The effective index is n=√ε∞. The vacuum wavenumber is 2π/λ₀. The optical path excess is (n−1)d, so multiply the excess by 2π/λ₀. Thickness and wavelength share units. Numerically, 2 * pi * (sqrt(4.26) - 1) * 2 / 1.55 ≈ 8.626 radians.
At equal slab and ambient indices the excess phase vanishes. A round trip would double the single-pass phase.

question: The calculated elastic data for Ta2C give Hill bulk modulus 255.963484 GPa and isotropic Poisson ratio 0.271140991. Determine the Hill shear modulus.
worked_solution:
Equate E=3K(1−2ν) to E=2G(1+ν). Solving for the shear modulus gives G=3K(1−2ν)/[2(1+ν)]. Inserting 255.963484 GPa and 0.271140991 gives the modulus in GPa. Numerically, 3 * 255.963484 * (1 - 2 * 0.271140991) / (2 * (1 + 0.271140991)) ≈ 138.25 GPa.
Positive elastic strain energy requires positive shear modulus. At fixed K a Poisson ratio approaching 1/2 implies small G relative to K.

question: A DFPT calculation for insulating Be2C gives the relaxed-ion relative permittivity diagonals 14.922223, 14.9216706, 14.921178. Determine the isotropic trace estimate appropriate to a static applied field.
worked_solution:
Use the relaxed-ion response because the field is static. One third of the trace gives ε₀,rel=(14.922223+14.9216706+14.921178)/3. Numerically, (14.922223 + 14.9216706 + 14.921178) / 3 ≈ 14.922.
A directional average of the diagonal static responses must lie within their range. It includes both the electronic and relaxed-ion contributions.

question: At 600 K consider the balanced reaction 2 BrK + 1 OTi → 1 K2O + 1 Br2Ti, using the indicated crystalline phases: BrK (Potassium Bromide), OTi (Titanium Oxide, Beta), K2O (Potassium Oxide), Br2Ti (Titanium Bromide). Treat the pure solids at unit activity. The standard molar formation enthalpies in kJ/mol are BrK -410.065, OTi -537.356, K2O -363.32, Br2Ti -431.412, and the formation Gibbs energies in the same order and units are -353.05, -481.621, -278.292, -337.615. Determine the signed entropy change for the written reaction.
worked_solution:
Apply the same stoichiometric products-minus-reactants sum to both sets of formation data. With matched temperature and elemental references, ΔrS°=(ΔrH°−ΔrG°)/T. Multiply by 1000 to express entropy in J/(mol K). The result is approximately -15.1 J/(mol of reaction K).
A standard molar entropy contributes once per mole of its phase in the balanced reaction. Reversing the reaction changes the sign of the entropy sum.

question: Apply the entropy formation relation with the following quantities. Hf = -74520 J/mol (Molar enthalpy of formation of the compound); Gf = -50490 J/mol (Molar Gibbs free energy of formation of the compound). Use T_ref = 298.15. In the units specified, use result = (Hf - Gf) / T_ref. Determine the entropy of formation of the compound in J/mol/K.
worked_solution:

question: For the following operating case, rated power = 2500 W; heating time = 1 h; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg·℃); mass of water = 40 kg; initial temperature = 20 ℃; final temperature = 70 ℃. Use the stated average or constant values over the same operating interval. Determine the thermal efficiency of the electric water heater.
worked_solution: Electric water heater energy consumption = rated power × heating time. Substitution gives (2500 W) × (1 h), or 2500 W·h. Heat absorbed by water = specific heat capacity of water × mass of water × increase in water temperature. Substitution gives (4200 J / (kg·℃)) × (40 kg) × (50 ℃), or 8400000 J. Thermal efficiency of the electric water heater = heat absorbed by water / electric water heater energy consumption. Substitution gives (8400000 J) / (2500 W·h), or 0.9333333 (dimensionless). In the requested unit this gives 93.3333 %. The result is approximately 93.333 %.

question: The calculated elastic data for Ca(ZnSi)2 give normal compliance trace 0.0290730952, sum S12+S13+S23 = -0.0073629905, and engineering shear compliance trace 0.0949302042, in GPa⁻¹. Determine the bulk modulus of the uniform-stress aggregate.
worked_solution:
Hydrostatic loading gives a volume compliance S11+S22+S33+2(S12+S13+S23). Its inverse is K_R. Numerically K_R = 1/[0.0290730952+2(-0.0073629905)] GPa. Numerically, 1 / (0.0290730952 + 2 * -0.0073629905) ≈ 69.7 GPa.
Hydrostatic loading applies equal normal stresses and no shear stresses. This is the uniform-stress estimate; a uniform-strain stiffness average describes another bound.

question: For a Cu1.98Se specimen at 1000.0 K, the reported Seebeck coefficient is 201.5 µV/K and electrical resistivity is 0.00325 Ω cm. Calculate the power factor.
worked_solution:
Power factor is S²/ρ. Convert microvolts to volts and Ω cm to Ω m before forming the ratio. Thus PF=(201.5×10⁻⁶)²/(0.00325×0.01) W/(m K²); the sign of S disappears. Numerically, (201.5 * 1e-06) ^ 2 / (0.00325 * 0.01) ≈ 0.0012493 W/(m K²).
S²/ρ equals S²σ. Apply the microvolt-to-volt factor before taking the square; a sign change of thermopower cannot change power factor.

question: For a Tl2SnTe5 specimen at 300.0 K, the total thermal conductivity is 5.09 W/(m K), ZT=0.067304238, and S=219.0 µV/K. Recover the electrical resistivity in Ω cm.

Changing only the sign of thermopower leaves the inferred resistivity unchanged because the transport figure uses its square.

question: For the following operating case, specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg·℃); mass of water = 0.5 kg; final temperature = 100 ℃; initial temperature = 20 ℃; current = 5 A; resistance = 40 Ω. Minimum heating time = heat absorbed by water / power of electric kettle during heating. Substitution gives (168000 J) / (1000 A²·Ω), or 168 J/(A²·Ω). The result is approximately 168 s.

question: A DFPT calculation for insulating PtO2 gives the electronic permittivity diagonals 9.75022129, 9.75031103, 2.82810962. Neglect magnetic response and absorption. Estimate the scalar optical index using the trace-averaged permittivity approximation.
worked_solution:
First take the electronic trace mean, ε∞=(9.75022129+9.75031103+2.82810962)/3. For μr≈1 the phase index satisfies n²=ε∞. Take the positive square root; the lattice contribution is excluded at optical frequencies. Numerically, sqrt((9.75022129 + 9.75031103 + 2.82810962) / 3) ≈ 2.7282.
This scalar approximates propagation in an optically averaged dielectric. Individual polarization eigenmodes of an anisotropic crystal need not share that index.

question: A DFPT calculation for insulating AlF3 gives the electronic relative permittivity diagonals 1.94254976, 1.94216596, 1.94401242. Determine the orientational mean for random electric-field directions.
worked_solution:
The mean directional response is one third of the trace. Off-diagonal terms vanish on orientation averaging. Thus ε∞=(1.94254976+1.94216596+1.94401242)/3. Numerically, (1.94254976 + 1.94216596 + 1.94401242) / 3 ≈ 1.9429.
The trace divided by three lies between the smallest and largest diagonal entries. The clamped-ion tensor excludes slow ionic relaxation.

question: For a Nd2Cu0.98Zn0.02O4 specimen at 700.0 K, the power factor is 4.042e-05 W/(m K²) and conductivity is 13.104 S/cm. What is the magnitude of the Seebeck coefficient?

question: At 800 K consider the balanced reaction 1 K2O4S + 1 F2Fe → 1 FeO4S + 2 FK, using the indicated crystalline phases: K2O4S (Potassium Sulfate, Alpha), F2Fe (Iron Fluoride), FeO4S (Iron Sulfate), FK (Potassium Fluoride). Treat the pure solids at unit activity. The standard molar formation enthalpies in kJ/mol are K2O4S -1439.835, F2Fe -700.813, FeO4S -929.15, FK -568.089, and the formation Gibbs energies in the same order and units are -1111.361, -594.541, -647.342, -486.915. Determine the signed entropy change for the written reaction.
worked_solution:
Apply the same stoichiometric products-minus-reactants sum to both sets of formation data. With matched temperature and elemental references, ΔrS°=(ΔrH°−ΔrG°)/T. Multiply by 1000 to express entropy in J/(mol K). The result is approximately -11.762 J/(mol of reaction K).
A standard molar entropy contributes once per mole of its phase in the balanced reaction. Reversing the reaction changes the sign of the entropy sum.

question: For crystalline Calcium Hydroxide (H2CaO2) at standard pressure, evaluated at 900 K, log₁₀ Kf = 42.134. Determine its standard molar Gibbs energy of formation using R=8.31446 J/(mol K).
worked_solution:
Kf is dimensionless on the standard-state scale. Convert the tabulated decimal logarithm to a natural logarithm, ln Kf=42.134 ln 10. Then ΔfG°=−RT ln Kf. Divide by 1000 for kJ/mol. Numerically, -8.31446 * 900 * 42.134 * log(10) / 1000 ≈ -725.98 kJ/mol.
A formation constant above one gives a negative standard formation Gibbs energy. Base-ten logarithms require the factor ln(10).

question: For a dense random polycrystal of YCu2, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 79.9975822 and 21.781768 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. A perfectly bonded thin film experiences equal imposed in-plane strains of 0.001 with the free surface under plane stress. What tensile stress develops in either in-plane direction?
worked_solution:
First convert the two aggregate moduli to Young's modulus: E=9KG/(3K+G)=59.908 GPa. Use ν=(3K−2G)/[2(3K+G)]=0.375188. Plane stress under equibiaxial strain gives σ=Eε/(1−ν); convert GPa to MPa. The result is approximately 95.882 MPa.
The out-of-plane surface carries no normal stress, while the bonded substrate imposes both in-plane strains. A uniaxial tensile modulus would miss the in-plane constraint.

question: The lattice vectors a and b of Ba3SbN are [7.66724, 0.0, 0.0] and [-3.83362, 6.640025, 0.0] Å in Cartesian coordinates. The cell volume is 343.916003 Å³. Find the spacing of adjacent (001) lattice planes in this cell basis.
worked_solution:
The area of the basal parallelogram is |a×b|=50.91067 Å². Translation by c increases the plane index by one, so the normal separation is V/|a×b| = 343.916003/50.91067 Å. It equals |c| only for c perpendicular to the basal plane. The result is approximately 6.7553 Å.
For an oblique cell only the component of the third lattice vector normal to the basal plane contributes to the spacing.

question: A tested steel has engineering yield strength 1798.3 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 2135.9 MPa, and elongation to fracture 6.0%. For a sheet coupon of initial width 12 mm and thickness 2.5 mm, find the increase in tensile load between first yield and maximum load.
worked_solution:
Use the same original area for both engineering strengths, A=12×2.5=30 mm². Since MPa is N/mm², ΔF=A(UTS−YS)=30(2135.9−1798.3) N; divide by 1000 for kN. Numerically, 30 * (2135.9 - 1798.3) / 1000 ≈ 10.128 kN.
Engineering stresses for both loads refer to the original area even after deformation begins. Using the necked area would mix engineering and true stress.

question: A homogeneous CaYb0.15Mn0.85O3 leg operates near 400 K. Treat the reported coefficients as constant over a small temperature difference. Its power factor is 6.7305e-05 W/(m K²). The length is 2 mm, area 1 mm² and temperature difference 10 K. Assume an ideal reference leg with zero thermopower and resistance. What power is delivered to a matched load?
worked_solution:
The open-circuit emf is SΔT, while internal resistance is L/(σA). Maximum electrical power is Voc²/(4R), hence PF·A·ΔT²/(4L). Convert mm² and mm to SI, then W to µW. Numerically, 6.7305e-05 * 1e-06 * 10 ^ 2 / (4 * 0.002) * 1000000.0 ≈ 0.84131 µW.
At a matched load half the open-circuit voltage appears across the load. Squaring that voltage and dividing by load resistance gives the delivered electrical power.

question: For crystalline Mercury Chloride (Cl2Hg2) at standard pressure, evaluated at 1000 K, S°=326.703 J/(mol K) and H°(T)−H°(298.15 K)=79.112 kJ/mol. Calculate −[G°(T)−H°(298.15 K)]/T.

question: A straight 500 mm rod has a 0.18 mm axial gap to a rigid stop at its free end; its other end is fixed. It is heated uniformly by 60 K. Use a linear expansion coefficient of 12e-6 per K and E=100 GPa. Neglect buckling, plasticity and stop compliance. What compressive stress magnitude develops?
worked_solution: Unconstrained expansion would be αLΔT = (12×10⁻⁶)(500)(60) = 0.36 mm, exceeding the 0.18 mm gap. The first 0.18 mm produces no stress; compatibility suppresses only the remaining 0.18 mm. The compressive elastic strain magnitude is 0.18/500 = 0.00036 and E times this strain is 36 MPa. With a gap at least as large as free expansion, the same heating would develop zero stress.

question: A DFPT calculation for insulating Ca2SnS4 gives the electronic relative permittivity diagonals 5.00251465, 4.82615293, 6.59713588. Determine the orientational mean for random electric-field directions.
worked_solution:
The mean directional response is one third of the trace. Off-diagonal terms vanish on orientation averaging. Thus ε∞=(5.00251465+4.82615293+6.59713588)/3. Numerically, (5.00251465 + 4.82615293 + 6.59713588) / 3 ≈ 5.4753.
The trace divided by three lies between the smallest and largest diagonal entries. The clamped-ion tensor excludes slow ionic relaxation.

question: A tested steel has engineering yield strength 1123.1 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 1247.1 MPa, and elongation to fracture 23.0%. For a sheet coupon of initial width 12 mm and thickness 2.5 mm, find the increase in tensile load between first yield and maximum load.
worked_solution:
Use the same original area for both engineering strengths, A=12×2.5=30 mm². Since MPa is N/mm², ΔF=A(UTS−YS)=30(1247.1−1123.1) N; divide by 1000 for kN. Numerically, 30 * (1247.1 - 1123.1) / 1000 ≈ 3.72 kN.
Engineering stresses for both loads refer to the original area even after deformation begins. Using the necked area would mix engineering and true stress.

question: For crystalline Nickel Sulfide (NiS2) at standard pressure, evaluated at 400 K, S°=93.015 J/(mol K) and −[G°(T)−H°(298.15 K)]/T=74.763 J/(mol K). Find the enthalpy increment above 298.15 K.
worked_solution:
Let Φ be the given Gibbs function. G=H−TS gives H(T)−H(298.15)=T(S−Φ). The entropy and Φ have identical units. Multiply their difference by 400 K and divide by 1000. Numerically, 400 * (93.015 - 74.763) / 1000 ≈ 7.3008 kJ/mol.
Use the same enthalpy reference in Φ and in ΔH; changing it shifts the inferred sensible enthalpy.

question: A tested steel has engineering yield strength 1019.7 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 1157.5 MPa, and elongation to fracture 15.0%. The fitted fracture pieces have a final gauge length of 62.0 mm. What initial gauge length is consistent with the elongation measurement?

The reported elongation is engineering strain based on original length. Lf/L0 = 1+15.0/100. Thus L0=62.0/(1+15.0/100) mm; a positive tensile elongation requires L0<62 mm. Numerically, 62 / (1 + 15.0 / 100) ≈ 53.913 mm.

question: The calculated elastic data for Mn3ZnC give C11+C22+C33 = 922.759431, C12+C13+C23 = 403.001625, and C44+C55+C66 = 186.907521 GPa in Voigt notation. Estimate the bulk modulus under the uniform-strain assumption.
worked_solution:
Equal normal strains load the three axes together. Averaging the hydrostatic stress and dividing by volumetric strain gives K_V=(C11+C22+C33+2C12+2C13+2C23)/9. Shear terms drop out. Insert (922.759431+2×403.001625)/9. Numerically, (922.759431 + 2 * 403.001625) / 9 ≈ 192.08 GPa.
A uniform dilatation produces three equal normal strains and zero shear strain. Off-diagonal normal stiffnesses enter twice; shear stiffnesses do not enter this average.

question: For the following operating case, water density = 1000 kg/m³; water volume = 2 L; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg·℃); mass of dry wood = 5 kg; calorific value of dry wood = 12000000 J/kg; final temperature = 85 ℃; initial temperature = 10 ℃. Use constant specific heat and assume no phase change in the heated sample. Treat the given fuel as completely burned. Use the ratio of useful output to supplied input for the indicated conversion. Treat the stated densities as uniform. Determine the efficiency of heating water with an iron pot.
worked_solution: Rise in temperature of water = final temperature-initial temperature. Substitution gives (85 ℃)-(10 ℃), or 75 ℃. Water mass = water density × water volume. Substitution gives (1000 kg / m³) × (2 L), or 2 kg. Heat absorbed by water = specific heat capacity of water × water mass × rise in temperature of water. Substitution gives (4200 J / (kg·℃)) × (2 kg) × (75 ℃), or 630000 J. Heat released by complete combustion of dry wood = mass of dry wood × calorific value of dry wood. Substitution gives (5 kg) × (12000000 J / kg), or 6e+07 J. Efficiency of heating water with an iron pot = heat absorbed by water / heat released by complete combustion of dry wood. Substitution gives (630000 J) / (60000000 J), or 0.0105 (dimensionless). In the requested unit this gives 1.05 %. The result is approximately 1.05 %.

question: Use an effective, transparent, nonmagnetic optical medium for NiF2, with trace-averaged electronic relative permittivity 2.52. At vacuum wavelength 1.55 µm, find the additional single-pass phase in radians through a 2.0 µm slab relative to the same distance in vacuum. Report the unwrapped phase.
worked_solution:
Use the electronic response at optical frequencies. The effective index is n=√ε∞. The vacuum wavenumber is 2π/λ₀. The optical path excess is (n−1)d, so multiply the excess by 2π/λ₀. Thickness and wavelength share units. Numerically, 2 * pi * (sqrt(2.52) - 1) * 2 / 1.55 ≈ 4.7627 radians.
At equal slab and ambient indices the excess phase vanishes. A round trip would double the single-pass phase.

question: For a dense random polycrystal of Mg2Si, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 52.8552189 and 44.5705496 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. An initially unstressed 10.0 cm³ specimen is slowly subjected to 100 MPa hydrostatic pressure. In the linear approximation find the stored elastic energy.
worked_solution:
Hydrostatic strain magnitude is p/K. The elastic energy per initial volume is the integral of pressure against volume strain, p²/(2K). Use p=10⁸ Pa, K=52.8552189×10⁹ Pa, V₀=10⁻⁵ m³. Numerically, 100000000.0 ^ 2 * 1e-05 / (2 * 52.8552189 * 1000000000.0) ≈ 0.94598 J.
The body starts unloaded; linear pressure increase gives half the final-pressure times the volume decrease.

question: For crystalline Phosphorus, Black (P) at standard pressure, evaluated at 900 K, S°=50.647 J/(mol K) and H°(T)−H°(298.15 K)=15.747 kJ/mol. Calculate −[G°(T)−H°(298.15 K)]/T.
worked_solution:
Use G°(T)=H°(T)−TS°. Relative to the fixed enthalpy reference the requested function is S°−[H°(T)−H°(298.15)]/T. The enthalpy increment must first be multiplied by 1000. Numerically, 50.647 - 15.747 * 1000 / 900 ≈ 33.15 J/(mol K).
At the enthalpy reference temperature the increment vanishes and the tabulated function equals the absolute molar entropy.

question: For crystalline Titanium Carbide (CTi) at standard pressure, evaluated at 400 K, the enthalpy increment over 298.15 K is 3.813 kJ/mol. The Gibbs energy function −[G°(T)−H°(298.15 K)]/T is 25.648 J/(mol K). Find S°(T).
worked_solution:
From H−G=TS, S° is the Gibbs function plus the enthalpy increment divided by T. The increment and the Gibbs function share the same reference. Thus S°=25.648+1000×3.813/400. Numerically, 25.648 + 1000 * 3.813 / 400 ≈ 35.181 J/(mol K).
An enthalpy increment and an absolute entropy use different reference conventions. At the enthalpy reference temperature the increment is zero, so Φ coincides with S°.

question: A DFPT calculation for insulating Li4NCl gives static tensor diagonals (10.8067683, 10.9350853, 8.35263109) and clamped-ion diagonals (4.06486685, 4.06887172, 3.98707929). Estimate the orientation-averaged relative permittivity due to ionic relaxation alone.
worked_solution:
The slow response contains both contributions. Subtract the high-frequency electronic part and average over directions: Δε=[(10.8067683−4.06486685)+(10.9350853−4.06887172)+(8.35263109−3.98707929)]/3. Numerically, (10.8067683 + 10.9350853 + 8.35263109 - (4.06486685 + 4.06887172 + 3.98707929)) / 3 ≈ 5.9912.
The difference isolates the response from ion relaxation. At optical frequencies these slower displacements cannot follow the field.

question: A DFPT stress-form piezoelectric tensor for NdHO2 gives e22 = -0.41193 C/m² in Cartesian axes. At zero electric field impose a compressive normal strain of magnitude 0.10% along axis 2, with all other strain components held at zero. What signed polarization change along axis 2 is predicted in µC/m²?
worked_solution:
Use the direct effect at fixed electric field, ΔP_i=Σ e_ik ε_k. Here only ε_2=-0.001 contributes. The given coefficient already uses polarization per unit strain. Multiplying -0.41193 by -0.001 gives C/m²; convert by 10⁶. Numerically, -0.41193 * -0.001 * 1000000.0 ≈ 411.93 µC/m².
A tensile-to-compressive strain reversal reverses the sign of the polarization increment at fixed electric field. Percent strain must be divided by 100 before contracting the tensor.

method: entropy rise with variable heat capacity
question: Heat one mole of crystalline Aluminum Iodide (AlI3) reversibly at constant pressure from 700 to 800 K. The measured or tabulated endpoint Cp values are 125.063 and 126.918 J/(mol K). Take Cp as linear in T over this single-phase interval. Find ΔS.
worked_solution:
Write Cp=a+bT with b=(126.918−125.063)/100 and a=125.063−b×700. Integrating Cp/T gives a ln[(800)/700]+100b. Kelvin is required in the logarithm. Numerically, (125.063 - (126.918 - 125.063) * 700 / 100) * log(800 / 700) + (126.918 - 125.063) ≈ 16.821 J/(mol K).
Because Cp is positive throughout the stated heating interval, the entropy rise is positive. The integral is of Cp/T rather than Cp alone.

method: mean isobaric heat capacity from entropy
question: For crystalline Niobium Carbide (C0.98Nb), S° rises from 64.616 to 72.038 J/(mol K) between 600 and 700 K. Estimate a single constant heat capacity that reproduces this entropy rise. Assume one phase and fixed pressure.
worked_solution:
For a constant effective Cp, ΔS=Cp ln(T₂/T₁). Divide the entropy difference by the natural logarithm of the absolute temperature ratio. Over a short interval this also approximates the enthalpy-based mean. Numerically, (72.038 - 64.616) / log(700 / 600) ≈ 48.148 J/(mol K).
This effective heat capacity uses a logarithmic temperature interval, because dS=Cp dT/T along a reversible isobaric path.

question: A reported Rb2O cell has edges a=7.39368982, b=9.91422556, c=9.91673882 Å and interaxial angles α=80.4013574, β=68.0988617, γ=138.168735 degrees. Calculate the cell volume without assuming orthogonal axes.

Take the scalar triple product of the lattice vectors. With u=cos α, v=cos β, w=cos γ, V=abc√(1+2uvw−u²−v²−w²). Substituting the stated edges and angles yields 312.816 Å³. The result is approximately 312.82 Å³.
The volume has cubic length units. If all three angles are right angles the metric determinant reduces to the product of the edge lengths squared.

method: recover sensible enthalpy from Gibbs function
question: For crystalline Mercury Oxide (HgO) at standard pressure, evaluated at 600 K, S°=104.632 J/(mol K) and −[G°(T)−H°(298.15 K)]/T=79.617 J/(mol K). Find the enthalpy increment above 298.15 K.
worked_solution:
Let Φ be the given Gibbs function. G=H−TS gives H(T)−H(298.15)=T(S−Φ). The entropy and Φ have identical units. Multiply their difference by 600 K and divide by 1000. Numerically, 600 * (104.632 - 79.617) / 1000 ≈ 15.009 kJ/mol.
Use the same enthalpy reference in Φ and in ΔH; changing it shifts the inferred sensible enthalpy.

question: For a dense random polycrystal of HfPd3, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 178.516568 and 84.6182697 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. An initially unstressed 10.0 cm³ specimen is slowly subjected to 100 MPa hydrostatic pressure. In the linear approximation find the stored elastic energy.
worked_solution:
Hydrostatic strain magnitude is p/K. The elastic energy per initial volume is the integral of pressure against volume strain, p²/(2K). Use p=10⁸ Pa, K=178.516568×10⁹ Pa, V₀=10⁻⁵ m³. Numerically, 100000000.0 ^ 2 * 1e-05 / (2 * 178.516568 * 1000000000.0) ≈ 0.28009 J.
The body starts unloaded; linear pressure increase gives half the final-pressure times the volume decrease.

question: At 600 K consider the balanced reaction 1 Be3N2 + 3 F2Mg → 3 BeF2 + 1 Mg3N2, using the indicated crystalline phases: Be3N2 (Beryllium Nitride, Alpha), F2Mg (Magnesium Fluoride), BeF2 (Beryllium Fluoride), Mg3N2 (Magnesium Nitride). Treat the pure solids at unit activity. The standard molar Gibbs energies of formation in kJ/mol are Be3N2 -476.039, F2Mg -1018.315, BeF2 -932.474, Mg3N2 -340.037. Find the signed standard Gibbs energy per reaction as written.
worked_solution:
Apply the stoichiometric sum of formation Gibbs energies, products minus reactants. All values refer to the same temperature and elemental reference states. The coefficients apply to the written reaction, not to one mole of each species. Numerically, -1 * -476.039 + -3 * -1018.315 + 3 * -932.474 + 1 * -340.037 ≈ 393.53 kJ/mol of reaction.
The sign is for the equation as written. Reversing every stoichiometric coefficient reverses ΔrG°.

question: For a dense random polycrystal of Nb, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 174.472038 and 19.8965503 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. A rod 75 mm long with section 20 mm² is loaded quasistatically from zero to 950 N in tension. Find the stored elastic energy.
worked_solution:
First convert the two aggregate moduli to Young's modulus: E=9KG/(3K+G)=57.5038 GPa. The stiffness is EA/L in N/mm after converting GPa to MPa. Linear loading stores half the final load times extension, U=F²L/(2EA). One N mm is one mJ. Numerically, 950 ^ 2 * 75 / (2 * 20 * 1000 * (9 * 174.472038 * 19.8965503 / (3 * 174.472038 + 19.8965503))) ≈ 29.427 mJ.
For a straight-line load–extension curve its area is half the final load times the final extension. N·mm converts directly to mJ.

For a dense random polycrystal of Nb, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 174.472038 and 19.8965503 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. A rod 75 mm long with section 20 mm² is loaded quasistatically from zero to 950 N in tension. Find the stored elastic energy.
Express the answer in this unit: mJ

Before the final answer line, give a concise worked solution with the governing equation, substitution with units, and the calculation.

First convert the two aggregate moduli to Young's modulus: E=9KG/(3K+G)=57.5038 GPa. The stiffness is EA/L in N/mm after converting GPa to MPa. Linear loading stores half the final load times extension, U=F²L/(2EA). One N mm is one mJ. Numerically, 950 ^ 2 * 75 / (2 * 20 * 1000 * (9 * 174.472038 * 19.8965503 / (3 * 174.472038 + 19.8965503))) ≈ 29.427 mJ.
For a straight-line load–extension curve its area is half the final load times the final extension. N·mm converts directly to mJ.
FINAL = 29.427

question: At 500 K consider the balanced reaction 1 B4K2O7 + 1 CNa2O3 → 1 CK2O3 + 1 B4Na2O7, using the indicated crystalline phases: B4K2O7 (Potassium Borate), CNa2O3 (Sodium Carbonate), CK2O3 (Potassium Carbonate), B4Na2O7 (Sodium Borate). Treat the pure solids at unit activity. The standard molar Gibbs energies of formation in kJ/mol are B4K2O7 -2999.075, CNa2O3 -990.4, CK2O3 -1004.553, B4Na2O7 -2946.574. Find the signed standard Gibbs energy per reaction as written.
worked_solution:
Apply the stoichiometric sum of formation Gibbs energies, products minus reactants. All values refer to the same temperature and elemental reference states. The coefficients apply to the written reaction, not to one mole of each species. Numerically, -1 * -2999.075 + -1 * -990.4 + 1 * -1004.553 + 1 * -2946.574 ≈ 38.348 kJ/mol of reaction.
The sign is for the equation as written. Reversing every stoichiometric coefficient reverses ΔrG°.

question: Apply the q rad relation with the following quantities. emissivity = 1 (dimensionless) (Fraction of black-body radiation which is emitted); T = 400 K (Temperature of the surface). Use T2 = 0, sigma = 5.670367e-08. In the units specified, use T_T = T * T, then T2_T2 = T2 * T2, then result = sigma * emissivity * (T_T * T_T - T2_T2 * T2_T2). Determine the heat exchange in W/m^2.
worked_solution:
Net thermal radiation depends on the difference of fourth powers of absolute temperatures. Equal surface and environmental temperatures give zero net flux.
T_T = 400 * 400 = 160000; T2_T2 = 0 * 0; result = 5.670367e-08 * 1 * (160000 * 160000 - 0 * 0) = 1451.61 W/m^2.

question: For the following operating case, volume of gasoline consumed = 8 L; density of gasoline = 710 kg/m^3; calorific value of gasoline = 46000000 J/kg; resistance = 653.2 N; travel distance = 100 km. Treat the given fuel as completely burned. Use the ratio of useful output to supplied input for the indicated conversion. Treat the stated densities as uniform. Determine the efficiency of the car.
worked_solution: Mass of gasoline consumed = volume of gasoline consumed × density of gasoline. Substitution gives (8 L) × (710 kg / m^3), or 5.68 kg. Heat released from gasoline consumed = mass of gasoline consumed × calorific value of gasoline. Substitution gives (5.68 kg) × (46000000 J / kg), or 2.6128e+08 J. Work done to overcome friction resistance per 100 km = resistance × travel distance. Substitution gives (653.2 N) × (100 km), or 65320 N·km. Efficiency of the car = work done to overcome friction resistance per 100 km / heat released from gasoline consumed. Substitution gives (65320 N·km) / (261280000 J), or 0.25 (dimensionless). In the requested unit this gives 25 %. The result is approximately 25 %.

question: The calculated elastic data for Sn give C11+C22+C33 = 177.950977, C12+C13+C23 = 84.2284259, and C44+C55+C66 = 79.0495085 GPa in Voigt notation. Estimate the Voigt upper bound on the isotropic shear modulus.
worked_solution:
The uniform-strain average combines the normal-stiffness difference with three shear terms. G_V = (ΣCii_normal − ΣCij_off + 3ΣCii_shear)/15 = (177.950977 − 84.2284259 + 3×79.0495085)/15 GPa. Numerically, (177.950977 - 84.2284259 + 3 * 79.0495085) / 15 ≈ 22.058 GPa.
The equal-strain average involves a normal-stiffness difference as well as shear stiffnesses. In the isotropic limit it reduces to the single shear modulus.

question: For the following operating case, hourly flow rate = 0.6 m^3/h; time = 1 h; water density = 1000 kg/m^3; temperature difference = 10 ℃; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg·℃); heating efficiency = 60 %. Use constant specific heat and assume no phase change in the heated sample. Use the ratio of useful output to supplied input for the indicated conversion. Treat the stated densities as uniform. Determine the effectively utilized heat.
worked_solution: Volume of water entering the radiator in 1 hour = hourly flow rate × time. Substitution gives (0.6 m^3 / h) × (1 h), or 0.6 m³. Water mass = water density × volume of water entering the radiator in 1 hour. Substitution gives (1000 kg / m^3) × (0.6 m³), or 600 kg. Heat released by hot water = specific heat capacity of water × water mass × temperature difference. Substitution gives (4200 J / (kg·℃)) × (600 kg) × (10 ℃), or 2.52e+07 J. Effectively utilized heat = heat released by hot water × heating efficiency. Substitution gives (25200000 J) × (60 %), or 1.512e+07 J. The result is approximately 1.512e+07 J.

question: The calculated elastic data for VRh give K_V = 233.088016, K_R = 233.005957, G_V = 103.877905, G_R = 87.6937556 GPa. Using the universal anisotropy index (five shear modes and one bulk mode), quantify the deviation from the isotropic limit.
worked_solution:
In an isotropic solid both upper/lower ratios are one. Subtract that six-mode baseline: A_U = 5G_V/G_R + K_V/K_R − 6 = 5(103.877905/87.6937556) + 233.088016/233.005957 − 6. The two ratios are dimensionless. Numerically, 5 * 103.877905 / 87.6937556 + 233.088016 / 233.005957 - 6 ≈ 0.92312.
Both Voigt-to-Reuss ratios are at least one for stable elastic data. Their weighted excess above one must vanish in the isotropic limit.

question: A DFPT calculation for insulating LiBeP gives the electronic relative permittivity diagonals 8.87032409, 8.87032409, 7.08333787. Determine the orientational mean for random electric-field directions.
worked_solution:
The mean directional response is one third of the trace. Off-diagonal terms vanish on orientation averaging. Thus ε∞=(8.87032409+8.87032409+7.08333787)/3. Numerically, (8.87032409 + 8.87032409 + 7.08333787) / 3 ≈ 8.2747.
The trace divided by three lies between the smallest and largest diagonal entries. The clamped-ion tensor excludes slow ionic relaxation.

method: entropy rise with variable heat capacity
question: Heat one mole of crystalline Molybdenum Oxide (MoO2.889) reversibly at constant pressure from 800 to 900 K. The measured or tabulated endpoint Cp values are 97.415 and 101.611 J/(mol K). Take Cp as linear in T over this single-phase interval. Find ΔS.
worked_solution:
Write Cp=a+bT with b=(101.611−97.415)/100 and a=97.415−b×800. Integrating Cp/T gives a ln[(900)/800]+100b. Kelvin is required in the logarithm. Numerically, (97.415 - (101.611 - 97.415) * 800 / 100) * log(900 / 800) + (101.611 - 97.415) ≈ 11.716 J/(mol K).
Because Cp is positive throughout the stated heating interval, the entropy rise is positive. The integral is of Cp/T rather than Cp alone.

method: shear modulus from bulk and contraction
question: The calculated elastic data for TiSiCu give Hill bulk modulus 148.392939 GPa and isotropic Poisson ratio 0.279318013. Determine the Hill shear modulus.
worked_solution:
Equate E=3K(1−2ν) to E=2G(1+ν). Solving for the shear modulus gives G=3K(1−2ν)/[2(1+ν)]. Inserting 148.392939 GPa and 0.279318013 gives the modulus in GPa. Numerically, 3 * 148.392939 * (1 - 2 * 0.279318013) / (2 * (1 + 0.279318013)) ≈ 76.793 GPa.
Positive elastic strain energy requires positive shear modulus. At fixed K a Poisson ratio approaching 1/2 implies small G relative to K.

question: A tested steel has engineering yield strength 1153.4 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 1359.8 MPa, and elongation to fracture 17.2%. The fitted fracture pieces have a final gauge length of 62.0 mm. What initial gauge length is consistent with the elongation measurement?
worked_solution:
The reported elongation is engineering strain based on original length. Lf/L0 = 1+17.2/100. Thus L0=62.0/(1+17.2/100) mm; a positive tensile elongation requires L0<62 mm. Numerically, 62 / (1 + 17.2 / 100) ≈ 52.901 mm.
Positive permanent elongation requires a smaller initial gauge length than the reassembled broken specimen.

question: For a dense random polycrystal of CrAgSe2, the Hill bulk and shear moduli are 63.6046298 and 22.9955874 GPa. Assume isotropic, small-strain elasticity. A perfectly bonded thin film experiences equal imposed in-plane strains of 0.001 with the free surface under plane stress. What tensile stress develops in either in-plane direction?
worked_solution:
First convert the two aggregate moduli to Young's modulus: E=9KG/(3K+G)=61.5671 GPa. Use ν=(3K−2G)/[2(3K+G)]=0.338672. Plane stress under equibiaxial strain gives σ=Eε/(1−ν); convert GPa to MPa. The result is approximately 93.096 MPa.
The out-of-plane surface carries no normal stress, while the bonded substrate imposes both in-plane strains. A uniaxial tensile modulus would miss the in-plane constraint.

question: At 600 and 700 K the standard formation reaction of crystalline Potassium Sulfate, Alpha (K2O4S) has log₁₀ Kf values 103.978 and 86.012. Assuming nearly constant reaction enthalpy and the same standard phases across this interval, estimate ΔfH°. Use R=8.31446 J/(mol K).
worked_solution:
The integrated van 't Hoff relation is ln(K₂/K₁)=−ΔH°(1/T₂−1/T₁)/R. Multiply the difference of decimal logarithms by ln 10. The slope versus inverse temperature gives the enthalpy with the minus sign. Numerically, -8.31446 * log(10) * (86.012 - 103.978) / (1 / 700 - 1 / 600) / 1000 ≈ -1444.6 kJ/mol.
Check the sign using the temperature dependence of K: an exothermic formation reaction has a smaller equilibrium constant at the higher temperature.

question: A homogeneous In1.9Ge0.1O3 leg operates near 300 K. Treat the reported coefficients as constant over a small temperature difference. Its power factor is 0.0002147 W/(m K²). The length is 2 mm, area 1 mm² and temperature difference 10 K. Assume an ideal reference leg with zero thermopower and resistance. What power is delivered to a matched load?
worked_solution:
The open-circuit emf is SΔT, while internal resistance is L/(σA). Maximum electrical power is Voc²/(4R), hence PF·A·ΔT²/(4L). Convert mm² and mm to SI, then W to µW. Numerically, 0.0002147 * 1e-06 * 10 ^ 2 / (4 * 0.002) * 1000000.0 ≈ 2.6837 µW.
At a matched load half the open-circuit voltage appears across the load. Squaring that voltage and dividing by load resistance gives the delivered electrical power.

A DFPT calculation for insulating PI2 gives the electronic relative permittivity diagonals 3.02407277, 3.6880849, 4.65777318. Determine the orientational mean for random electric-field directions.
Express the answer in this unit: dimensionless

Before the final answer line, give a concise worked solution with the governing equation, substitution with units, and the calculation.

The mean directional response is one third of the trace. Off-diagonal terms vanish on orientation averaging. Thus ε∞=(3.02407277+3.6880849+4.65777318)/3. Numerically, (3.02407277 + 3.6880849 + 4.65777318) / 3 ≈ 3.79.
The trace divided by three lies between the smallest and largest diagonal entries. The clamped-ion tensor excludes slow ionic relaxation.
FINAL = 3.79

question: At 700 K consider the balanced reaction 1 O4V2 + 3 O3Ti2 → 2 O5Ti3 + 1 O3V2, using the indicated crystalline phases: O4V2 (Vanadium Oxide), O3Ti2 (Titanium Oxide), O5Ti3 (Titanium Oxide, Beta), O3V2 (Vanadium Oxide). Treat the pure solids at unit activity. The standard molar formation enthalpies in kJ/mol are O4V2 -1408.212, O3Ti2 -1509.833, O5Ti3 -2436.818, O3V2 -1210.125, and the formation Gibbs energies in the same order and units are -1185.426, -1320.542, -2137.514, -1035.245. Determine the signed entropy change for the written reaction.
worked_solution:
Apply the same stoichiometric products-minus-reactants sum to both sets of formation data. With matched temperature and elemental references, ΔrS°=(ΔrH°−ΔrG°)/T. Multiply by 1000 to express entropy in J/(mol K). The result is approximately 24.53 J/(mol of reaction K).
A standard molar entropy contributes once per mole of its phase in the balanced reaction. Reversing the reaction changes the sign of the entropy sum.

question: A DFPT stress-form piezoelectric tensor for KRb2ZrOF5 gives e33 = 0.22978 C/m² in Cartesian axes. At zero electric field impose a tensile normal strain of magnitude 0.10% along axis 3, with all other strain components held at zero. What signed polarization change along axis 3 is predicted in µC/m²?
worked_solution:
Use the direct effect at fixed electric field, ΔP_i=Σ e_ik ε_k. Here only ε_3=0.001 contributes. The given coefficient already uses polarization per unit strain. Multiplying 0.22978 by 0.001 gives C/m²; convert by 10⁶. Numerically, 0.22978 * 0.001 * 1000000.0 ≈ 229.78 µC/m².
A tensile-to-compressive strain reversal reverses the sign of the polarization increment at fixed electric field. Percent strain must be divided by 100 before contracting the tensor.

question: Apply the calc Cmax relation with the following quantities. mh = 22.0 kg/s (Mass flow rate of hot stream); mc = 5.5 kg/s (Mass flow rate of cold stream); Cph = 2200 J/kg/K (Averaged heat capacity of hot stream); Cpc = 4400.0 J/kg/K (Averaged heat capacity of cold stream). In the units specified, use Ch = mh * Cph, then Cc = mc * Cpc, then result = max(Ch, Cc). Determine the the heat capacity rate of the larger fluid in W/K.
worked_solution:
Compare the two mass-flow times specific-heat products. The larger heat-capacity rate undergoes the smaller temperature change for the same duty.
Ch = 22 * 2200 = 48400; Cc = 5.5 * 4400 = 24200; result = max(48400, 24200) = 48400 W/K.

question: The calculated elastic data for BeCu give Voigt and Reuss bounds of K_V = 142.229604, K_R = 142.229595, G_V = 84.4859043, G_R = 54.9113954 GPa. For a randomly oriented polycrystal treated as isotropic, estimate Poisson's ratio using Hill's prescription.
worked_solution:
Average like bounds before combining moduli: K = (142.229604+142.229595)/2 = 142.23 GPa and G = (84.4859043+54.9113954)/2 = 69.6986 GPa. The isotropic relation is ν = (3K−2G)/[2(3K+G)]. The units cancel. The result is approximately 0.28938.
For an isotropic aggregate with positive bulk and shear moduli the result must be between −1 and 1/2. Young's modulus inferred from 2G(1+ν) must agree with 3K(1−2ν).

question: At 600 K consider the balanced reaction 3 INa + 1 AlF6Li3 → 1 AlF6Na3 + 3 ILi, using the indicated crystalline phases: INa (Sodium Iodide), AlF6Li3 (Lithium Hexafluoroaluminate), AlF6Na3 (Cryolite, Alpha), ILi (Lithium Iodide). Treat the pure solids at unit activity. The standard formation Gibbs energies in kJ/mol are INa -268.035, AlF6Li3 -3061.477, AlF6Na3 -2982.666, ILi -256.948. Calculate log₁₀ K for the reaction as written. Use R=8.31446 J/(mol K).
worked_solution: Use signed stoichiometric amounts, positive for products. The sum of formation Gibbs energies is ΔrG° = (-3)×(-268.035) + (-1)×(-3061.477) + (1)×(-2982.666) + (3)×(-256.948) = 112.072 kJ/mol of reaction. Thus log₁₀K = −ΔrG°/(RT ln 10) = −(112.072×1000)/(8.31446×600×ln 10) = -9.756547. The sign of ΔrG° requires K less than one for the reaction as written.

question: The calculated elastic data for HfIr3 give S22 = 0.00405446011 GPa⁻¹. Load only along the Cartesian y axis of the tensor. All other stress components vanish. What is the directional Young modulus?
worked_solution:
The free transverse faces impose uniaxial stress, so the longitudinal strain is S22σ. Therefore E=σ/ε=1/S22=1/0.00405446011 GPa. Numerically, 1 / 0.00405446011 ≈ 246.64 GPa.
Free transverse faces impose zero transverse stress. The same longitudinal strain under lateral confinement can require a different stress.

question: For a Ca0.9Nd0.1MnO3 specimen at 700.0 K, S=-123.85 µV/K, electrical conductivity is 57.452 S/cm and total thermal conductivity is 2.41558 W/(m K). Estimate the dimensionless figure of merit.
worked_solution:
σ=57.452×100 S/m. The power factor is (-123.85×10⁻⁶)²σ. Multiplying by absolute temperature and dividing by total thermal conductivity gives ZT=S²σT/κ. Numerically, (-123.85 * 1e-06) ^ 2 * (57.452 * 100) * 700.0 / 2.41558 ≈ 0.025537.
Use one temperature scale in kelvin. S²σ gives the power factor in W/(m·K²), and multiplication by T followed by division by κ gives a dimensionless result.

question: A Cartesian-axis compliance measurement for VRu gives S11=0.00665920178 and S21=-0.00273016771 GPa⁻¹. Under uniaxial tensile stress along x with free lateral faces, determine the signed Poisson ratio describing strain along y.
worked_solution:
In the compliance form, εx=S11σx and εy=S21σx because all other stresses vanish. By definition νxy=−εy/εx=−(-0.00273016771)/0.00665920178. Numerically, --0.00273016771 / 0.00665920178 ≈ 0.40998.
The strain ratio uses the loading-direction compliance in its denominator. Interchanging the two directions generally changes the answer in a single crystal.

method: mean isobaric heat capacity from entropy
question: For crystalline Cobalt Oxide (CoO), S° rises from 80.628 to 90.497 J/(mol K) between 500 and 600 K. Estimate a single constant heat capacity that reproduces this entropy rise. Assume one phase and fixed pressure.
worked_solution:
For a constant effective Cp, ΔS=Cp ln(T₂/T₁). Divide the entropy difference by the natural logarithm of the absolute temperature ratio. Over a short interval this also approximates the enthalpy-based mean. Numerically, (90.497 - 80.628) / log(600 / 500) ≈ 54.13 J/(mol K).
This effective heat capacity uses a logarithmic temperature interval, because dS=Cp dT/T along a reversible isobaric path.

question: At 400 K consider the balanced reaction 1 B6Li2O10 + 2 INa → 1 B6Na2O10 + 2 ILi, using the indicated crystalline phases: B6Li2O10 (Lithium Borate), INa (Sodium Iodide), B6Na2O10 (Sodium Borate), ILi (Lithium Iodide). Treat the pure solids at unit activity. The standard molar Gibbs energies of formation in kJ/mol are B6Li2O10 -4288.034, INa -282.898, B6Na2O10 -4207.071, ILi -269.208. Find the signed standard Gibbs energy per reaction as written.
worked_solution:
Apply the stoichiometric sum of formation Gibbs energies, products minus reactants. All values refer to the same temperature and elemental reference states. The coefficients apply to the written reaction, not to one mole of each species. Numerically, -1 * -4288.034 + -2 * -282.898 + 1 * -4207.071 + 2 * -269.208 ≈ 108.34 kJ/mol of reaction.
The sign is for the equation as written. Reversing every stoichiometric coefficient reverses ΔrG°.

question: A homogeneous Ca2.7Bi0.3Co4O9 leg operates near 400 K. Treat the reported coefficients as constant over a small temperature difference. Electrical conductivity is 98.464 S/cm. A 5 mm long leg with a 2 mm² cross section is held at uniform temperature. The maximum voltage drop is 0.12 V and the maximum allowed Joule heat rate is 0.006 W. What is the largest steady current in amperes?
worked_solution: In an isothermal leg there is no Seebeck voltage. Uniform current gives R=L/(σA)=0.005/[(98.464×100)(2×10⁻⁶)] = 0.2539 Ω. The voltage limit allows Vmax/R = 0.472627 A. The heating limit allows √(Pmax/R) = 0.153725 A. Both must hold, so heating limits the current to 0.153725 A. At this current the voltage is 0.0390307 V and the heat rate is 0.006 W.

question: For the following operating case, specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg·℃); mass of water = 5 kg; temperature increase of water = 50 ℃; volume of natural gas = 0.035 m^3; calorific value of natural gas = 40000000 J/m^3. Use constant specific heat and assume no phase change in the heated sample. Treat the given fuel as completely burned. Use the ratio of useful output to supplied input for the indicated conversion. Determine the efficiency of natural gas in heating water.
worked_solution: Heat absorbed by water = specific heat capacity of water × mass of water × temperature increase of water. Substitution gives (4200 J / (kg·℃)) × (5 kg) × (50 ℃), or 1050000 J. Heat released from burning natural gas = volume of natural gas × calorific value of natural gas. Substitution gives (0.035 m^3) × (40000000 J / m^3), or 1400000 J. Efficiency of natural gas in heating water = heat absorbed by water / heat released from burning natural gas. Substitution gives (1050000 J) / (1400000 J), or 0.75 (dimensionless). In the requested unit this gives 75 %. The result is approximately 75 %.

question: For the following operating case, density of water = 1000 kg/m^3; volume of water = 5 L; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg⋅℃); thermal efficiency = 10 %; calorific value of charcoal = 34000000 J/kg; final temperature = 98 ℃; initial temperature = 30 ℃. Use constant specific heat and assume no phase change in the heated sample. Treat the given fuel as completely burned. Use the ratio of useful output to supplied input for the indicated conversion. Treat the stated densities as uniform. Determine the mass of charcoal required.
worked_solution: Temperature increase of water = final temperature-initial temperature. Substitution gives (98 ℃)-(30 ℃), or 68 ℃. Mass of water = density of water × volume of water. Substitution gives (1000 kg / m^3) × (5 L), or 5 kg. Heat absorbed by water = specific heat capacity of water × mass of water × temperature increase of water. Substitution gives (4200 J / (kg⋅℃)) × (5 kg) × (68 ℃), or 1428000 J. Heat released by burning charcoal = heat absorbed by water / thermal efficiency. Substitution gives (1428000 J) / (10 %), or 1.428e+07 J. Mass of charcoal required = heat released by burning charcoal / calorific value of charcoal. Substitution gives (14280000 J) / (34000000 J / kg), or 0.42 kg. The result is approximately 0.42 kg.
